paper_metadata.title: Clinical features and treatment outcomes of Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy patients

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study provides a clear description of the recruitment setting, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and baseline characteristics. Recruitment was continuous, and the sample size is relatively large for this specific epilepsy syndrome.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: All study populations consisted of epilepsy patients from the Department of Neurology at West China Hospital between October 2012 and July 2014.
items.reasoning: The source population is clearly defined as patients from a specific neurology department in a major hospital.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: We continuously reviewed one hundred and five outpatients with JME who were diagnosed and treated at the Epilepsy Registration Center of West China Hospital
items.reasoning: Continuous recruitment from a specialized registration center reduces selection bias compared to convenience sampling.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between October 2012 and July 2014.
items.reasoning: The dates for the recruitment window are explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Department of Neurology at West China Hospital... Chengdu, 610041, China.
items.reasoning: The specific hospital and geographic location are provided.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: The inclusion criteria were as follows: (a) the diagnosis of JME on the basis of ILAE criteria... The exclusion criteria were as follows: (a) abnormal CT/MRI presentation; (b) unexpected death... (c) development of intracranial infection...
items.reasoning: Detailed inclusion and exclusion criteria are listed, including the use of international diagnostic standards (ILAE).

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Finally, 105 JME patients were included in this study.
items.reasoning: The study accounts for excluded patients (2 deaths, 5 poor adherence), suggesting a high participation rate among those eligible.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: We reviewed the demographic and clinical data of the patients, including age, gender, age of seizure onset, age at diagnosis, duration of epilepsy, seizure type, AED treatment, family history, and social outcome
items.reasoning: Table 1 provides a comprehensive breakdown of baseline characteristics for the study sample.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study reports very low attrition. Only 7 patients were excluded from the initial screening, and follow-up methods (clinic and telephone) were used to maintain data collection for the remaining 105.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: All patients in this study were followed up every 3‐6 months until July 2017.
items.reasoning: The study implies full follow-up for the 105 included patients through the end of the study period.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: When patients could not return to the hospital for follow‐up, they were followed up by telephone.
items.reasoning: The use of telephone interviews to supplement clinic visits is a standard method to minimize attrition.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: Two patients were excluded due to death... Five patients were excluded because of poor drug adherence
items.reasoning: Reasons for exclusion/dropout prior to the final cohort assembly are clearly stated.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While reasons for exclusion are given, the specific baseline characteristics of the 7 excluded patients are not compared to the 105 included patients.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no formal analysis comparing completers vs. non-completers, though the number of non-completers is very small (n=7).

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factors (seizure types and AED types) are well-defined and measured using standard clinical and EEG criteria consistently across the cohort.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: The seizure type of JME was myoclonic seizure (MS), which could be combined with generalized tonic‐clonic seizure (GTCS)... or absence seizure (AS)
items.reasoning: Prognostic factors (seizure types) are defined according to ILAE standards.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The diagnosis of patients with JME was decided by two neurologists according to clinical review, medical records, and EEG recordings.
items.reasoning: Diagnosis and factor identification relied on expert review and objective EEG data.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: The median dose (mg, d) VPA... 556.8... 1250.0
items.reasoning: Doses and ages are reported as continuous means/medians.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Every time the study population visited the neurologists, new medical information was recorded on case‐record forms.
items.reasoning: Standardized data collection was used for all participants at the same center.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: Finally, 105 JME patients were included in this study.
items.reasoning: The analysis includes the full cohort for the primary prognostic factors.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not mention missing data for prognostic factors or the use of imputation.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (seizure freedom) is clearly defined, but measurement relies heavily on patient/parent recall (clinic visits and telephone interviews) without mention of seizure diaries or blinding, which introduces potential for recall bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: The remission group was defined as having had no seizure for at least 12 months at the last follow‐ up time
items.reasoning: The primary outcome (remission) is explicitly defined with a temporal threshold.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Seizure status and AED treatment and withdrawal were evaluated every 3‐6 months by clinic visits or telephone interview.
items.reasoning: Measurement relies on self-reporting/recall. There is no mention of blinding the assessors to the prognostic factors (seizure type/AED).

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Every time the study population visited the neurologists, new medical information was recorded on case‐record forms.
items.reasoning: The follow-up schedule and recording methods were standardized for the cohort.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study does not perform multivariable adjustment. While it compares groups on baseline characteristics, it relies on univariable analyses (Chi-square, t-tests) to link factors to outcomes, failing to account for the interplay between seizure type, AED choice, and dosage.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: We reviewed the demographic and clinical data of the patients, including age, gender, age of seizure onset, age at diagnosis, duration of epilepsy, seizure type, AED treatment, family history
items.reasoning: Key potential confounders were collected at baseline.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Median dose (mg, d) VPA... LEV...
items.reasoning: Confounders like medication dose and duration of epilepsy are defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The diagnosis... was decided by two neurologists according to clinical review, medical records, and EEG recordings.
items.reasoning: Confounders related to clinical history were verified through medical records.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Every time the study population visited the neurologists, new medical information was recorded on case‐record forms.
items.reasoning: Consistent data collection setting for all participants.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: No mention of missing data handling for confounders.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The study is a prospective cohort without matching or stratification in the design phase.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: Chi‐square tests or Fisher's exact tests were used for group comparisons... Nonparametric data were analyzed by the Mann‐Whitney U and t tests.
items.reasoning: The analysis is limited to univariable tests. No multivariable regression (e.g., Cox or Logistic) was performed to adjust for confounding.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical methods are basic and do not include survival analysis (e.g., Kaplan-Meier), which is standard for 'time to event' or 'seizure freedom' data. However, the reporting is transparent regarding the results obtained.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Microsoft Excel 2013® and SPSS version 20 software (SPSS Inc.) were used for statistical analyses.
items.reasoning: The tools and specific tests used are clearly listed.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There was no multivariable model building strategy described.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Chi‐square tests or Fisher's exact tests were used for group comparisons
items.reasoning: While Chi-square is okay for simple proportions, it does not account for follow-up time or censoring, making it less than ideal for longitudinal prognosis.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: The 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year seizure-free rates of the patients were 64.8% (68/105), 29.5% (31/105), and 14.6% (12/82), respectively.
items.reasoning: The study reports outcomes at multiple time points and for different subgroups as planned.
